objectives: Distinguish DRAM from SRAM + their characteristics.
Reason about NAND flash + storage trade-offs.

slides.title: Cache hierarchy + locality
slides.body:
Memory hierarchy: cheap+big+slow at the bottom, expensive+small+fast at the top.

**Modern CPU hierarchy** (approximate, e.g., Apple M3 / AMD Zen 4):
- **Registers**: ~16-256 per core, 64-bit each. ~0 cycle access.
- **L1 cache**: ~32-64 KB per core. ~4 cycles. Split into I-cache + D-cache.
- **L2 cache**: ~512 KB - 2 MB per core. ~10-15 cycles.
- **L3 cache**: ~8-128 MB shared. ~30-40 cycles.
- **DRAM**: ~16-512 GB. ~150-300 cycles.
- **SSD / NVMe**: TBs. ~30,000+ cycles (100 μs).
- **HDD**: TBs. millions of cycles (10 ms).

**Locality of reference**:
- **Temporal**: recently accessed data likely to be re-accessed soon. Caches exploit by KEEPING recently-used data.
- **Spatial**: nearby addresses likely to be accessed. Caches exploit by FETCHING in cache-line granularity (~64 bytes typically).

**Cache architecture**:
- **Cache line / block**: unit of data movement, typically 64 bytes.
- **Set-associative**: each address can map to one of K 'ways' in a 'set'. Common: 4-way, 8-way, 16-way.
- **Replacement policy**: which way to evict on miss. LRU (Least Recently Used) is common.
- **Inclusive vs exclusive**: inclusive = lower levels contain all of higher (simpler invalidation, more redundancy). Exclusive = mutually exclusive (more capacity, more complex).

**Cache miss types** (Hill's '3 Cs'):
- **Compulsory** (cold): first access to a block. Unavoidable.
- **Capacity**: cache too small to hold working set. Bigger cache helps.
- **Conflict**: cache-mapping collisions. Higher associativity helps.

**Programmer impact**:
- Sequential access > random (spatial locality).
- Loop tiling / blocking improves locality (BLAS).
- Avoid pointer-chasing on huge data structures.
- 'Cache-conscious' algorithms (B-trees vs binary trees) match cache line sizes.

slides.title: DRAM + SRAM + emerging memories
slides.body:
**SRAM (Static RAM)** — what caches are made of:
- 6 transistors per bit (6T cell).
- Holds value as long as powered.
- Fast (~ns) + low power per access.
- Expensive: ~6× area of DRAM per bit.

**DRAM (Dynamic RAM)** — main memory:
- 1 transistor + 1 capacitor per bit (1T1C). Tiny cell.
- Capacitor leaks → must be REFRESHED every ~64 ms.
- Cheaper + denser than SRAM.
- Slower access (~50-100 ns).
- DDR4 / DDR5 / LPDDR (low-power for mobile).

**DRAM hierarchy** (within a chip):
- **Bank**: independent sub-array. 8-32 banks per DRAM chip.
- **Row / column**: 2D array. Access row first (activate) → then read columns.
- **Bank conflicts** + **row-buffer hits/misses**: another level of locality. Sequential access within a row is fast; switching rows = expensive precharge + activate.

**HBM (High Bandwidth Memory)** — used in modern GPUs + accelerators:
- 3D-stacked DRAM dies, with TSVs (Through-Silicon Vias).
- High bandwidth (TBps).
- Used in NVIDIA H100/H200, AMD MI300, Apple M2 Ultra UltraFusion.

**NVDIMM / Optane** (deprecated 2022):
- Phase-change-memory hybrid. Persistent + DRAM-like.
- Killed by economics (Intel discontinued).

**Emerging**:
- **MRAM (Magnetic RAM)**: non-volatile, fast write. Embedded in some SoCs.
- **ReRAM (Resistive RAM)**: similar profile; used in ML inference + analog computing.
- **Compute-in-memory**: do matrix-multiply directly in DRAM/SRAM cells. Eliminates fetch energy. Active research (Mythic, Crossbar, Samsung experimental).

**Memory bandwidth wall**: as cores + accelerators get faster, memory bandwidth doesn't keep up. Modern AI workloads are memory-bandwidth-bound (large weight transfers per matrix multiply). HBM + on-package DRAM (Apple's unified memory, NVIDIA Grace+Hopper) try to address.

slides.title: NAND flash + storage trade-offs
slides.body:
**NAND flash**: non-volatile storage. Cells trap charge in floating gates.

**Cell types**:
- **SLC (Single-Level Cell)**: 1 bit/cell. Fast, durable (~100K writes). Expensive.
- **MLC (Multi-Level)**: 2 bits/cell. Slower, less durable (~3K writes).
- **TLC**: 3 bits/cell. ~1K writes.
- **QLC**: 4 bits/cell. ~100-500 writes. Cheapest.

Density vs durability trade-off. Consumer SSDs: TLC mostly, QLC for cheap models.

**3D NAND**: stack ~100-200+ layers. Modern SSDs use 3D-TLC or 3D-QLC. Yields TB-per-die capacity.

**SSD-specific issues**:
- **Write amplification**: a 4 KB write may require erasing + rewriting an entire BLOCK (~MB). Garbage collection + wear leveling crucial.
- **TRIM**: OS tells SSD which blocks are unused; SSD can erase pre-emptively.
- **Lifespan**: in TB-Written. Consumer SSDs: 600-1200 TBW for 1 TB. Enterprise: 5-10× more.

**Interfaces**:
- **SATA**: ~600 MB/s. Legacy.
- **NVMe (over PCIe)**: ~3-12 GB/s (PCIe 3.0 / 4.0 / 5.0). The modern standard.
- **U.2 / M.2 / E1.S**: form factors.

**Storage classes today** (price + performance, 2024):
- HDD: \$15/TB. ~150 MB/s. Cold storage.
- TLC SSD: \$50-80/TB. ~3-7 GB/s.
- QLC SSD: \$40-60/TB. ~1-3 GB/s sustained writes; bursts faster.
- DRAM: \$3-5/GB (~10× more expensive than SSD per GB).

**Tape**: \$5/TB. Still in use for archive (LTO-9 = 18 TB native).

**Trade-offs for system design**:
- Bandwidth bound? DRAM > NVMe > HDD by orders of magnitude.
- Latency bound? DRAM ~100 ns, NVMe ~50 μs (500×), HDD ~10 ms (100,000×).
- Capacity? HDD > QLC SSD > TLC SSD > DRAM > caches.
- Durability? SLC > MLC > TLC > QLC. SLC for cache; QLC for read-mostly bulk.

question.question: Compute Average Memory Access Time (AMAT)
question.goal: L1 cache: 4 cycle hit, 5% miss rate. L2 cache: 12 cycle hit, 25% miss rate. DRAM: 200 cycles.

steps.prompt: AMAT = HitTime_L1 + MissRate_L1 × MissPenalty_L1. MissPenalty_L1 = HitTime_L2 + MissRate_L2 × MissPenalty_L2. MissPenalty_L2 = DRAM time = 200. So MissPenalty_L1 = ?
If L1 miss rate doubled to 10%, AMAT becomes?
steps.reveal: AMAT = 10.2 cycles. Doubling L1 miss rate increased AMAT by 43%. L1 hit rate is THE most important cache metric.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{AMAT} = \text{HitTime} + \text{MissRate} \times \text{MissPenalty}}$$ The recursive formula extends to N cache levels. Modern systems with 4-5 levels (registers, L1, L2, L3, DRAM, optionally NVMe) compute AMAT layer by layer. The huge gap between cache hits (~ns) + DRAM/SSD (~100ns/100μs) makes cache hierarchy fundamental to performance. Every additional level halves typical access cost — pivotal for ML / database / GPU workloads.

question.question: ML training is increasingly 'memory-bandwidth-bound'. Why?
options: Modern compute (FLOPs) grows faster than memory bandwidth (FLOPS/byte ratio increases). Each matrix-multiply requires fetching massive weight + activation tensors. Bandwidth bottleneck dominates. Mitigations: HBM, on-package memory, sparse models, mixed precision.
question.explanation: FLOPs/sec growth: ~50%/year (Moore's-law-ish). Memory bandwidth growth: ~30%/year. The gap widens. Modern ML workloads pull GBs of weights per second. NVIDIA H100 has 80 GB HBM3 at 3.35 TB/s; even this bottlenecks large training runs. Solutions: 1) HBM (3D-stacked DRAM next to compute); 2) lower-precision (fp8, int8) halves data movement; 3) sparse + quantized models; 4) compute-in-memory. The 'memory wall' has been a major architectural focus for the last decade.

hints: What's the FLOPs vs bandwidth gap?
slides.workedSolution: FLOPs grow faster than bandwidth historically. Modern ML: each FLOP needs roughly 1 byte of data (matrix-multiply data reuse is limited). Result: model size grows → bandwidth becomes binding. Architectural responses: 1) HBM next-to-die, 2) on-package DRAM (Apple M-series), 3) low-precision data formats (fp8/int8), 4) sparsity (Mixture-of-Experts activates only some weights per token), 5) compute-in-memory experimental. All are responses to the bandwidth wall.

Choosing storage for a data center
question.prompt: Your data center needs 10 PB of storage for a workload that's 80% reads + 20% writes. Walk through whether to use QLC SSD, TLC SSD, or HDD-tier.
Explain in two or three sentences why a CPU spends ~50% of its die area on caches.
question.rubric: Mentions that DRAM access takes 100-300 cycles while cache hits take ~4-30; without caches the CPU spends ~95% of time waiting for memory; large + well-designed caches turn most accesses into hits + keep the CPU pipeline full. The 50% die-area allocation reflects how much performance comes from memory hierarchy.
